# About this tutorial

Before looking for hits, check that the screen worked: that every sample was
sequenced deeply enough, that the library was not lost, and that replicates
agree. A problem found here (a failed replicate, a bottleneck) would otherwise
produce false hits later.

This is the second of three tutorials. It starts from the object built in
**1. Getting your data into ScreenR**:

```{r object, message=FALSE}
library(ScreenR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

data(count_table)
data(annotation_table)

counts <- count_table
colnames(counts) <- c(
    "Barcode", "Time1", "Time2", "Time3_TRT_A", "Time3_TRT_B", "Time3_TRT_C",
    "Time3_CTRL_A", "Time3_CTRL_B", "Time3_CTRL_C",
    "Time4_TRT_A", "Time4_TRT_B", "Time4_TRT_C",
    "Time4_CTRL_A", "Time4_CTRL_B", "Time4_CTRL_C"
)
counts <- filter(counts, Barcode != "*")
groups <- factor(c(
    "T1/T2", "T1/T2",
    rep("Time3_TRT", 3), rep("Time3_CTRL", 3),
    rep("Time4_TRT", 3), rep("Time4_CTRL", 3)
))

object <- create_screenr_object(
    table = counts, annotation = annotation_table, groups = groups
)
object <- remove_all_zero_row(object)
object <- normalize_data(object)
object <- compute_data_table(object)
```

Many plots accept a `palette`, one color per sample. Here replicates of the
same condition share a color:

```{r palette}
palette <- c(
    "#66c2a5", "#fc8d62", rep("#8da0cb", 3), rep("#e78ac3", 3),
    rep("#a6d854", 3), rep("#ffd92f", 3)
)
```

| Step | Question | Functions |
|------|----------|-----------|
| 1 | Was each sample sequenced deeply enough? | `mapped_reads()`, `plot_mapped_reads()` |
| 2 | Are the counts distributed similarly in all samples? | `plot_mapped_reads_distribution()` |
| 3 | How many barcodes were lost? | `barcode_lost()`, `plot_barcode_lost()`, `plot_barcode_lost_for_gene()` |
| 4 | Do replicates agree? | `plot_replicate_correlation()` |
| 5 | Is the library still evenly represented? | `compute_gini()`, `plot_gini()` |
| 6 | Do samples cluster by condition? | `plot_mds()`, `plot_pca()`, `plot_explained_variance()` |
| 7 | Which normalization should I use? | `normalize_data()` |

# Step 1: sequencing depth

The number of reads assigned to barcodes in each sample.

```{r mapped-reads}
mapped_reads(object)
plot_mapped_reads(object, palette = palette) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

**What to look for.** All samples should have a similar number of reads, and
enough for the size of the library: a common rule of thumb is at least a few
hundred reads per barcode on average (here about 5300 barcodes, so about
1.5 million reads or more). A sample with far fewer reads than its replicates
is less reliable. Different depths are corrected by the normalization; very low
depth is not. Here every sample has between about 7 and 12 million reads;
`Time3_TRT_A` has fewer reads than its replicates but still more than 1000 per
barcode, which is enough.

# Step 2: distribution of the counts

```{r distribution}
plot_mapped_reads_distribution(object, palette = palette,
    alpha = 0.8, type = "boxplot"
) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
plot_mapped_reads_distribution(object, palette = palette,
    alpha = 0.4, type = "density"
)
```

**What to look for.** The distributions should have a similar shape. A sample
whose distribution is much wider or shifted may have had a technical problem
(for example during PCR amplification).

# Step 3: lost barcodes

A barcode is lost in a sample when it has zero reads. Some loss over time is
expected in a dropout screen; a large loss means that the library was not
represented well enough (too few cells per barcode).

```{r barcode-lost}
barcode_lost(object)
plot_barcode_lost(object, palette = palette) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

To see which genes lost barcodes in some samples:

```{r barcode-lost-gene, fig.height = 6}
plot_barcode_lost_for_gene(object, samples = c("Time3_TRT_A", "Time4_TRT_A"))
```

**What to look for.** A few lost barcodes per sample are normal. A gene that
lost most of its barcodes in all samples, including the controls, was not
represented well and its results are unreliable.

# Step 4: agreement between replicates

`plot_replicate_correlation()` shows the correlation of the log2 counts per
million between every pair of samples.

```{r correlation, fig.height = 6}
plot_replicate_correlation(object)
```

**What to look for.** Replicates of the same condition (the blocks along the
diagonal) should be the most correlated samples. A replicate with a low
correlation to its partners may be an outlier: check it in the next plots
before deciding whether to remove it.

# Step 5: evenness of the library

The Gini index measures how unevenly the reads are spread over the barcodes:
0 means that every barcode has the same number of reads, 1 that a single
barcode has all of them.

```{r gini}
compute_gini(object)
plot_gini(object, palette = palette)
```

**What to look for.** In a dropout screen the Gini index usually increases
slowly over time, as some barcodes are depleted. A sudden jump, or a large
difference between replicates, suggests a bottleneck (too few cells were kept
at some step). Here it increases from about 0.42 to 0.48: a normal trend.

# Step 6: overall structure of the samples

The multidimensional scaling (MDS) plot places similar samples close to each
other. By default the points are labelled by sample:

```{r mds}
plot_mds(object)
```

The `groups` argument colors the samples by any variable, for example by
treatment or by time point:

```{r mds-groups}
samples <- get_sample_table(object)

plot_mds(object, groups = factor(samples$Treatment))
plot_mds(object, groups = factor(samples$Day))
```

`plot_pca()` shows the samples on the components of a principal component
analysis of the log2 normalized counts (with the normalization chosen in
`normalize_data()`), with the share of the variability
each component explains on the axes; `components` selects other components.
Unlike the MDS, which uses the most variable barcodes, it uses all of them,
so the two plots are a check of each other:

```{r pca}
plot_pca(object)
plot_pca(object, groups = factor(samples$Treatment))
```

`plot_explained_variance()` shows how much of the variability each principal
component explains (`cumulative = TRUE` for the cumulative proportion).

```{r explained-variance}
plot_explained_variance(object)
plot_explained_variance(object, cumulative = TRUE)
```

**What to look for.** Replicates should be close to each other. Samples usually
separate first by time point (cells change as they grow) and then by
treatment. A replicate far from its group is a candidate outlier.

In this dataset the samples separate by time point along the first dimension,
as expected. Two treated replicates at Time4, `Time4_TRT_B` and
`Time4_TRT_C`, are far from the other samples along the second dimension;
`Time4_TRT_B` also has the most lost barcodes and the lowest correlations with
the other samples. They are worth a closer look. Removing a replicate should
be justified by a technical reason; otherwise keep it, and use the
replicate-aware methods of tutorial 3, which take this variability into
account.

# Step 7: choosing the normalization

`normalize_data()` offers three methods:

| Method | Divides the counts of each sample by | Use it when |
|--------|--------------------------------------|-------------|
| `"cpm"` (default) | Its total number of reads | Most screens |
| `"tmm"` | Its total number of reads, corrected with the edgeR TMM factors | Strong hits deplete a large part of the library, so the total is biased |
| `"control"` | The reads of control barcodes (e.g. non-targeting shRNAs) | The library has control barcodes that are not affected by the treatment |

A quick way to decide between `"cpm"` and `"tmm"` is to compare them: if they
agree, the default is fine.

```{r normalization}
object_tmm <- normalize_data(object, method = "tmm")
ratio <- colMeans(SummarizedExperiment::assay(object_tmm, "normalized")) /
    colMeans(SummarizedExperiment::assay(object, "normalized"))
tibble(Sample = names(ratio), TMM_over_CPM = round(ratio, 3))
```

Here the two methods differ by at most about 2%, so we keep the default. With
control barcodes the call would be
`normalize_data(object, method = "control", control_barcodes = my_controls)`,
where `my_controls` is the vector of their identifiers.

The normalization affects the frequencies, the Z-scores and the plots. The
edgeR-based methods of tutorial 3 (CAMERA, ROAST) always model the raw counts
and do their own normalization. After changing the normalization, run
`compute_data_table()` again.

# Checklist

* [ ] Every sample has enough reads, and replicates have similar depths.
* [ ] Few barcodes were lost, especially in the control samples.
* [ ] Replicates are highly correlated and close in the MDS plot.
* [ ] The Gini index increases smoothly, with similar values for replicates.
* [ ] You chose a normalization and re-computed the data table if you changed
  it.

The next tutorial, **3. Finding and validating hits**, uses this object.
